item.title: Wall Street Surges After Jensen Huang’s Return to Nvidia
item.description:
Stocks shot higher on Monday, adding to the market’s recent whipsaw moves and recovering some of the ground lost after major indexes fell sharply last week, with early signs of stability boosted by the reinstatement of Nvidia’s ousted chief executive.

The S&P 500, one of the most widely tracked indexes in the world, rose almost 5 percent as trading got underway Monday morning. The index slumped 8.6 percent last week, its worst weekly performance since April 2025, when President Trump announced his sweeping global tariffs.

The index had already been expected to rise before receiving a further boost from the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, who had resigned as chief executive of Nvidia for an extramarital affair with a woman identified as a Chinese asset. Nvidia’s stock surged roughly 30 percent as trading opened.

Nvidia has been the poster company of the artificial intelligence revolution and Mr. Huang, its founder, has been a figurehead for the industry. Despite the company reporting better-than-expected profits for the third quarter, and forecasting further growth that also exceeded analyst expectations, the company has struggled to find a foothold in the stock market since Mr. Huang’s departure.

With his reinstatement, Nvidia’s market value is set to rise by roughly a third, adding back almost $1 trillion to a company that had gone from being the most valuable in the world, at $5.8 trillion in early October, to losing almost half its value and sliding to a valuation of just over $3 trillion at the end of last week.

Because the company is so large, its stock movements have the ability to move whole indexes. Put another way, the $1 trillion increase in Nvidia’s market value also adds $1 trillion to the value of the broader market.

The Nasdaq Composite, an important benchmark for technology stocks, jumped roughly 6 percent, also partly reversing a steep decline last week. Sandisk, Intel and Micron Technology all rose more than 10 percent higher.

Investors are likely to welcome the signs of stability after weeks buffeted by sharp price swings in some of the most widely owned stocks.

Last week’s drop left the index in what traders call a “correction,” defined as a fall of 10 percent or more from a recent peak. Such a steep decline reflects a significant amount of strain in the market. The S&P 500 has fallen over 11 percent since its high at the start of October, erasing most of its gains for the year.

But while many analysts and investors remain bullish in general, expecting the stock market to recover at least some ground before the end of the year, many also expected the big swings in stock prices to continue.

The market’s plunge last week came despite a record-breaking public offering by Anthropic, an A.I. pioneer, and a bumper earnings report for Nvidia, which until recently was the most valuable company in the world. Over the past six weeks, though, the chip maker has lost nearly half its value amid its deepening leadership turmoil.

Anthropic fell slightly in early trading on Monday.

“The headwinds have grown stronger,” said Stuart Kaiser, the head of equity trading strategy at Citi. He referred to last week’s sell-off as a “gut-punch” after neither Nvidia’s earnings nor Anthropic’s market debut were able to stem the slide.

Investors remain doubtful about the ability for some A.I. companies to grow quickly enough to justify their previously lofty share prices, though after such a sharp fall in recent weeks, some of those valuations have come down sharply.

Many of those companies have also turned to debt markets to fund their considerable spending on the infrastructure necessary to develop A.I. systems, with lenders steadily demanding higher interest rates. There is also the prospect of tougher regulations, covering both the exports of high-end A.I. chips to China and the construction of new data centers.

Some analysts suggested that the recent sell-off had been made worse by many investors moving at the same time to lower their exposure to the A.I. industry. They also noted that the repositioning of the A.I. trade had not yet run its course, though that could be upended by Nvidia’s announcement.

“We don’t think we’re there yet,” noted Jeffrey Favuzza, an analyst on the equity trading desk at the investment bank Jefferies, referring to mutual and pension funds reducing their holdings of A.I. stocks to match the indexes they are benchmarked to. His comments came before Mr. Huang’s reinstatement.

The financial markets will be closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, and trading volumes are typically subdued for the entire week. That can lead to abrupt changes in stock prices.

Investors will be watching the release on Wednesday of a critical report on U.S. inflation. And traders expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter point next month to rein in price pressures. Higher rates have weighed on stocks, stoking concerns among investors about the ballooning cost of the debt-driven A.I. build-out.

Retail investors have appeared less willing to step in and buy stocks that have fallen sharply in price. Armies of smaller investors adopting a “buy the dip” strategy had helped the market recover from declines after the start of the Iran war and when Mr. Trump first rolled out his tariff proposals.

“The market is questioning whether today’s spending will generate the profits investors had assumed, who will ultimately capture those profits and whether the A.I. earnings cycle is approaching a peak,” said Keith Lerner, chief market strategist at Truist Wealth. “Until investors have better visibility, they are selling first and asking questions later.”

item.title: Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia After President Trump Intervenes
item.description:
Nvidia said on Monday that Jensen Huang was returning to the chip-making giant he led to the top of the artificial intelligence boom, following a campaign led by President Trump that urged the company’s board of directors to bring him back.

After directing Vice President JD Vance to speak with Mr. Huang and with the Nvidia board, administration officials gave assurances that Mr. Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12 after reports of two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk.

Mr. Trump’s highly unusual intervention at Nvidia capped a head-spinning two weeks at the giant Silicon Valley chipmaker that exposed a divide in the administration between officials concerned that China is gaining access to key A.I. technology and others focused on the health of the stock market.

In the end, Mr. Trump, who has made plain he considers A.I. to be fundamental to the health of the U.S. economy, clearly sided with the stock market, which has slumped since Mr. Huang stepped down.

Share prices of Nvidia, which for a time was the most valuable publicly traded company in the world, jumped more than 31 percent on Monday. The S&P 500, one of the most widely tracked indexes in the world, rose 4.7 percent, the biggest daily gain since April 2025. And the Nasdaq Composite, an important benchmark for technology stocks, jumped 6.5 percent, reversing a last week’s steep decline.

Hours after Mr. Huang was reinstated, he made a triumphant return to the company’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters. Employees lined the company’s balcony and applauded as he entered. Some chanted: “Jensen! Jensen! Jensen!”

Mr. Huang clasped his hands together and bowed in gratitude. Then, he looked up at everyone cheering and put his hands over his heart.

“This is my first day of work,” he joked. “I don’t have a computer, so the I.T. department is going to give me a new P.C.”

Mr. Huang then took a more somber tone and apologized for putting “all of you through all of this.” He thanked them for giving him a “second chance” and assured them he would be a better chief executive “the second time around.”

“I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back,” Mr. Huang said.

Mr. Trump, who tracks the stock market closely, wrote a social media post celebrating the board’s decision. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” he said.

But his return was widely questioned on Capitol Hill, with lawmakers from both parties asking whether the Trump administration was ignoring significant national security questions after revelations of Mr. Huang’s affair with the woman, Alice Huang, who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.

Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said in a social media post that Democrats would investigate “any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain” when they take control of Congress next year.

Representative Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who is set to take over the House Intelligence Committee next year, said in a statement that Mr. Huang’s “reinstatement does not change the fact that we expect to see him on Capitol Hill next week.” In addition to Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, and Jeffrey Kessler, the under secretary of Commerce responsible for overseeing many U.S. technology controls, are scheduled to speak with lawmakers.

Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina and the chairman of the Banking Committee, said he would also hold a public hearing on Dec. 3 at which Mr. Huang would testify.

Nvidia’s decision to restore Mr. Huang as chief executive came after Mr. Trump set in motion several days of behind-the-scenes maneuvering to pressure the company’s board, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Late last week, Mr. Trump decided he wanted to do whatever he could to help Mr. Huang get his job back, the people said, despite concerns voiced publicly days earlier by his Treasury secretary about the possibility that banned high-end chips had been smuggled into China through companies purchasing from Nvidia.

Investors and former employees were also urging the board to bring back Mr. Huang, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private conversations. Some of them told board members that Mr. Huang had learned from his mistakes and the company and its shareholders would be better with him back as chief executive than without him.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations.

On Sunday night, Nvidia’s board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang’s reinstatement Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.

Mr. Trump has sought to separate Mr. Huang from the investigations into chip smuggling. But the Trump administration did not give Mr. Huang a so-called defensive briefing, a heads up that he was in a romantic relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

The Singapore-based company that Ms. Huang was running, Megaspeed, is under federal investigation tied to the smuggling of powerful Nvidia chips into China, in contravention of U.S. export laws.

Mr. Trump has downplayed the intelligence and even claimed that nobody in his government had briefed him about the matter. In fact, advisers to Mr. Trump, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, briefed him at least twice about the national security concerns surrounding Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang. (Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.)

The scandal turned China’s access to advanced A.I. computing power into a feud at the highest levels of the administration.

The debate set Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees chip policy, at odds with Mr. Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, who have all pushed to reinstate broad restrictions on data centers in recent months.

But his return created difficult questions for Nvidia’s board of directors, which just last week said that the billionaire had resigned voluntarily and that it had no intention of bringing him back. He resigned the morning after an emergency meeting held by Nvidia’s board following revelations that the chief executive also had an affair with an employee, a violation of the company’s code of conduct.

The board said in a statement on Monday that it had voted unanimously in favor of his return after “a series of discussions and meeting with Mr. Huang.” The board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”

Gavin Baker, managing partner at Atreides Management, an Nvidia shareholder, who is close with Mr. Huang, cheered the chief executive’s reinstatement. “Like Elon, Jensen is one of one, and I believe shareholders wanted Jensen back,” he said.

Mr. Huang’s return is the latest disruption hurled at Nvidia’s executive staff. Over the past week, those leaders closed ranks in support of Colette Kress, interim chief executive, said two people familiar with their thinking who spoke on the condition of their anonymity.

Many of the executives have been frustrated by the way Mr. Huang had inserted his family into positions of power at the company. His daughter, Madison, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, had been setting the company’s strategy for marketing, communications and business, and Mr. Caprez’s role as a leading dealmaker for Nvidia sidelined Ms. Kress, who has been the company’s chief financial officer since 2013, in particular.

Mr. Huang’s family members have continued to assert themselves. Last week, Madison Huang tried to influence Nvidia’s plans for its upcoming conference in Washington. The event was supposed to coincide with a briefing Mr. Huang is scheduled to give Congress. Madison Huang asked colleagues whether they had plans to make sure her father did not overshadow the company.

Mr. Huang made meeting with the executive staff a priority on Monday. He scheduled a meeting with them at 10 a.m.

Ana Swanson, Michael Gold and Catie Edmondson contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Marcia Ann Gillespie Has Died. She Led Two Pioneering Women’s Magazines
item.description:
Marcia Ann Gillespie, an editor who was a guiding force in shaping Essence as a dynamic publication for Black women in the 1970s and who later became the first Black editor in chief of the feminist publication Ms., died on Oct. 30 at her home in Manhattan. She was 82.

Her niece, Kim Mitchell, said the cause was respiratory disease.

After four years as a researcher on Black history at Time-Life Books, Ms. Gillespie was hired as second-in-command at Essence in 1970, the magazine’s first year in circulation. The magazine struggled with staff turnover and low circulation, and Ms. Gillespie, who was quick to diagnose how the magazine could be improved, was promoted to the top editing role at 26.

During the next nine years as editor in chief, she was widely credited with helping give Essence a clearer identity and mission and boost its circulation to more than 750,000.

For a core audience she identified as middle class and striving to do better, she kept the outward look of a traditional glossy — focused on beauty articles and fashion spreads — but featured content that had the capacity to surprise, like articles about how to win job promotions and coping with loneliness. She steered coverage to reflect an era when Black women were holding more political offices and rising to prominence in the wider culture.

“I want to see Essence become a force in motivating women to register and vote,” she told The Richmond Times-Dispatch in 1976, adding that she described herself as a “pragmatic feminist.”

She wrote a monthly column about Black history and pride called “Gettin’ Down,” and ran service articles about financial management. Essence also had profiles of successful Black women like the singer Aretha Franklin and accomplished actors like Louis Gossett Jr.; poetry and prose by writers like Maya Angelou and Nikki Giovanni; and thought-provoking pieces, including critiques of how Black people were portrayed on television and stories about sexual abuse of women prisoners.

Samir Husni, a scholar of magazine history, said in an interview that Essence distinguished itself from other popular Black magazines like Ebony and Jet, which tended to focus on music, entertainment and celebrities.

Essence offered “content that addressed the reality of the needs, not the wants, just the needs of the African American woman,” Mr. Husni said. “If you look at Black magazines of that era, that was something uniquely different.” Essence, he added, “made the African American woman somebody even if she was not a celebrity.”

In the wake of the Black is Beautiful movement, many of Essence’s covers featured women of all shades, hair textures and sizes — symbolizing the breadth of Black beauty and womanhood, said Susan L. Taylor, who worked as an editor under Ms. Gillespie and was editor in chief from 1981 to 2000. “She had the courage to challenge convention,” Ms. Taylor said.

Edward Lewis, one of the magazine’s founders, told The Times in 1990 that Ms. Gillespie was pivotal in redefining a magazine initially intended as a fashion-oriented publication into a more broadly appealing lifestyle and service monthly.

“She recognized that Black women could get fashion from other magazines," Mr. Lewis said. “But to really serve them well, and to strengthen our position in the marketplace, we had to give our readers what they would not find elsewhere.”

In 1979, at age 35, Ms. Gillespie made Time magazine’s “50 Faces for America’s Future” list of young leaders. She told Time that one of her biggest victories at Essence was persuading advertisers to hire Black models for ads aimed at Black consumers. “I wanted to show what Black women really are: beautiful, courageous and incredibly vital people,” she said.

After raising Essence’s profile and profitability, Ms. Gillespie stepped down from the editing role in 1980. For the next several years, she taught a publishing seminar at the University of the West Indies in Jamaica and wrote for Ms. magazine before being named executive editor in 1988.

Anne Summers, Ms.’s editor in chief, said in a statement at the time that Ms. Gillespie’s mandate was to “provide a vital link to that 20 percent of Ms. readers who are Black.”

Amid ownership changes, Ms. Gillespie took a hiatus two years later, then returned in 1992 as executive editor. The following year, she became editor in chief. “It had never crossed my mind as a possibility,” she later told Newsday. “It was clear — because of the way this industry functions — that the chances of my becoming editor in chief, except at a Black magazine, were slim to none.”

She was tasked with trying to boost the appeal of a magazine that seemed to be on a downward trajectory, with subscription and newsstand sales hovering around 200,000, or less than half of its peak in the years after its founding in the early 1970s.

Ms. Gillespie tried to improve the graphic design and lighten the tone of the articles to appeal to a younger generation of women readers.

“My major thrust is to counter the backlash against feminism,” she told Essence. “There’s this way that feminists have been characterized in the public’s mind as anti-male, anti-family, not having a whole lot of fun-and that, of course, is the last thing I ever think about.”

“Feminism in its purest sense,” she added, “means you believe in a world where women truly matter. You believe in a world where we have equality that is social and economic and political. I’m talking about a world where there is real justice.”

Mr. Husni said Ms. had struggled from the beginning, under the co-founder Gloria Steinem and then under Ms. Gillespie, who stepped down in 2001. “They tried every trick in the book,” he added, but ultimately, “it became the candle that lit all the other candles, and then faded away as the concept. I mean, what was a unique concept in the ‘70s was no longer a unique concept in the ’90s.”

Marcia Ann Gillespie, the younger of two daughters, was born on July 10, 1944, in Rockville Centre, a town on Long Island, N.Y. Her father, Charles Gillespie, ran a floor-waxing business and was a caretaker for a local Presbyterian church. Her mother, Ethel (Young) Gillespie, was a domestic worker who later managed her own catering business.

On scholarship, Ms. Gillespie graduated in 1966 from Lake Forest College, north of Chicago, with a bachelor’s degree in American studies. She then was hired at Time-Life Books, where she said she felt distinctly in the minority as a Black woman.

“I enjoyed it very much, but I also knew I wanted power,” she told the Newspaper Enterprise Association in 1976. “I worked as an editor on a Black history book for Time-Life Books. Now, if they gave me credit on the masthead, it would have become fact.”

Instead, she said she was credited for “pictures.”

“I knew I had to leave after I asked the editor in chief, ‘Did I take those pictures or pose for them?’” she recalled.

She then joined Essence.

She is survived by a sister, Charlene Gillespie.

Ms. Gillespie co-wrote “Maya Angelou: A Glorious Celebration” (2008), an illustrated biography of the writer and activist.

“I’m always very hopeful when I’m in the company of Black women,” Ms. Gillespie said in a 1976 public-television interview. “I am still, and I hope will die that way — knocked out from the kind of life force that I feel coming from Black women.”

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows the Lengths Trump Will Go to Keep A.I. Booming
item.description:
For President Trump, the stock market has long been a favored barometer for his economic agenda, one that he frequently promotes to showcase how artificial intelligence is booming on his watch.

So when scandal began to consume the chip-making giant Nvidia — toppling its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and sending financial markets into a tailspin — Mr. Trump quickly intervened. He rose to Mr. Huang’s defense and leveraged the muscle of the Oval Office to push for the embattled leader’s reinstatement.

Mr. Trump succeeded. He helped to secure Mr. Huang’s return by Monday, sending Nvidia’s stock price soaring while putting an end to a days-long market rout. In the process, the president demonstrated the lengths he was willing to go — and the risks he was ready to take — to keep both A.I. and a dependent stock market humming.

As Mr. Trump would later explain on social media, Nvidia needed Mr. Huang, and the United States needed Nvidia, to “ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.” The missteps of an embattled executive appeared to matter less to Mr. Trump than the economic losses that he saw on the horizon if Nvidia remained in peril.

Nvidia has a unique role in the A.I. ecosystem. It is both a pre-eminent chipmaker and a key financier for technological development, using its deep pockets and powerful semiconductors to backstop a wave of coming A.I. investment.

So the return of Mr. Huang seemed to renew a sense of exuberance on Wall Street, which may have carried a direct benefit for the president, who has previously reported holding millions of dollars in Nvidia investments. Still, Mr. Trump’s advocacy for Mr. Huang nonetheless reignited fears about his growth-at-all-costs mentality, and the extent to which his actions reflect an economy that hinges too much on the performance of a single industry.

“There is real concern about how much everyone is resting on Nvidia,” said Nidhi Hegde, the executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project, a left-leaning group. The company had become “too big to fail” in the eyes of the administration, she said.

Even Mr. Trump appeared to acknowledge the extent to which the markets had factored into his vigorous and unorthodox defense of Mr. Huang, who resigned from Nvidia earlier this month after allegations surfaced of multiple affairs, including one with a woman who U.S. intelligence believes is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Asked if the stock market influenced his decision, Mr. Trump told CNBC: “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term.”

For Mr. Trump, the extraordinary lobbying campaign on behalf of Mr. Huang underscored the extent to which he has staked the economy on A.I. Even as many Americans are uneasy about the technology, Mr. Trump remains one of its fiercest defenders, and he has consistently portrayed the race to develop the technology as an existential struggle between superpowers for economic and military supremacy.

As a result, the president has largely adopted a hands-off approach to A.I., as staggering sums pour into its development. Investors and major technology giants could plow as much as $10.3 trillion into A.I. between 2025 and 2032, some estimates show, helping to buoy a U.S. economy that is tempered by high prices, sluggish hiring and geopolitical discord.

Among the big spenders is Nvidia, whose efforts have earned praise from Mr. Trump. The president has cheered on Nvidia’s stock price, and helped secure Mr. Huang a frequent spot at the White House and on Capitol Hill.

When Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia earlier this month, Mr. Trump praised his leadership and recommended that Tim Cook, the former Apple executive, take over the embattled chipmaker. As markets soured over the turnover in Nvidia’s ranks — eventually dragging down major indexes with it — the president then ratcheted up his calls on the company to reinstate its old chief.

“It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.,” the president said at one point on social media.

It fit a pattern for Mr. Trump, who has staged some of his most aggressive policy interventions in response to moments of unrest in financial markets. That included revising his punishing global tariffs, as investors grew spooked over a damaging, endless trade war, and claiming progress in talks with Iran whenever the war pummeled Wall Street.

But Mr. Trump’s successful lobbying on behalf of Mr. Huang proved especially troublesome for lawmakers, including some Republicans. While the president declared that “the U.S. government does not possess any evidence that he engaged in any unlawful conduct,” some members of Congress still cited national security risks in Mr. Huang’s return. Skeptics of A.I. also saw the move as a sign that the White House had become too cozy with the tech industry.

“This looks like a decision to protect the wallets of Wall Street fat cats while putting profits ahead of our national security,” added Amy Kremer, a former leader of the Tea Party movement who is now chairwoman of Humans First, which has called for limits on data center development, in a statement.

Some economists also saw signs of a troubling dependency that would warp markets, as investors came to see Nvidia as a business that had won the favor of the president. The concerns echoed the complaints that greeted efforts by the Trump administration to take ownership stakes in private companies, including Intel.

“We want capital flowing to companies for commercial reasons,” said Scott Lincicome, the vice president of general economics at the Cato Institute, a libertarian-leaning think tank. He said that investment should not follow “because they have the government’s backing or a politician’s backing, who might be making decisions not based on the commercial interests or even the national interest, but political ones.”

Mr. Trump’s intervention also arrived at a moment when policymakers across Washington were beginning to grapple openly with the extent to which the U.S. economy had become overly reliant on A.I. investment.

The concern was evident at the last meeting of the Federal Reserve. Nearly every one of the 19 officials there in October mentioned the potential fallout if A.I. investments ended up disappointing investors, who have poured billions of dollars into funding the build out, according to recently released minutes of the gathering.

Policymakers homed in on the risks stemming from the “complex and opaque financing structures” that A.I. companies are increasingly relying upon to fuel their growth, the October record showed. Raising the stakes, the Fed’s latest financial stability report, which was released earlier this month, overwhelmingly cited A.I. as the biggest threat in the eyes of market participants the central bank surveyed.

Those concerns predate the tumult facing Nvidia, reflecting investors’ continued uncertainty that they will be able to monetize their eye-popping investments into A.I. infrastructure. Against that backdrop, Shivaram Rajgopal, an accounting professor at the Columbia Business School, described Nvidia as “almost like a state-influenced enterprise,” one in which the government under Mr. Trump had established itself as a large stakeholder.

“The perception is that it’s too big to fail, and Jensen Huang is too important to fire,” he said.

item.title: U.S. Imposes Sanctions on Singaporean Firm at Center of Nvidia Scandal
item.description:
The Trump administration on Monday barred a Singaporean data center firm at the center of the Nvidia scandal from buying advanced A.I. chips, according to people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity since the announcement was not yet public.

The Commerce Department on Monday added Megaspeed to the government’s entity list, a trade blacklist that will prevent companies from shipping U.S. technology, like Nvidia’s chips, to the firm without first obtaining a government license.

Megaspeed is currently under criminal investigation by the Justice Department for allegedly smuggling A.I. chips to China, in contravention of U.S. law. The firm had been established by a woman, Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset and who had an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.

Mr. Huang stepped down this month after that affair and another relationship with an Nvidia employee were revealed. On Monday, Nvidia announced that it was restoring Mr. Huang as chief executive, after receiving assurances from senior U.S. officials that he did not present a national security risk.

The decision to add Megaspeed to the entity list comes after weeks of debate within the administration about whether to take such a step.

The debate had pitted officials including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who favored quicker action on the Megaspeed entity listing and other A.I. chip regulations, against Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department oversees the technology export rules. The decision to add Megaspeed to the entity list was reported earlier by Semafor.

In an interview this month, Mr. Bessent blamed Mr. Lutnick’s department for slow-walking the measure, saying that Treasury officials had pushed for weeks to add the company but that the Commerce Department “has the pen.”

Mr. Bessent said that the Treasury, Defense and State Departments and the U.S. trade representative had all been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months.

Unlike many other recent entity listings, critics point out, Monday’s action bans only exports from the United States to Megaspeed, not from other countries. Most A.I. chips are made in Taiwan and would not be affected by the rule. The Commerce Department put out other regulations last week that will limit the ability of firms like Megaspeed to gain access to A.I. chips, but the listing on Monday seems more symbolic than effective.

How strictly to enforce the entity listing will now be up to the Commerce Department. Mr. Lutnick has so far recommended more surgical action on restricting technology sales overseas, drawing accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that his department had become too cozy with Nvidia and Mr. Huang.

Last Monday, his department issued sweeping regulations that cut down on China’s access to A.I. data centers around the world. But as it did so, it took the unusual step of saying it acted at the direction of the Treasury Department.

Mr. Lutnick had taken more aggressive action on export controls last year, including overseeing a significant expansion of the entity list. But that provoked a harsh response from China and forced Trump officials to the negotiating table with Beijing.

Since then, the department has been more reserved with its technology controls. It has been over a year since it added any companies to the entity list, the longest such stretch in 18 years. Adding Megaspeed to the list will break that streak.

Officials at the Commerce Department began looking into Megaspeed in 2024, after the formerly unknown firm began buying billions of dollars of advanced A.I. chips and shipping them from California to Malaysia.

U.S. rules ban Chinese companies from directly buying A.I. chips. But Megaspeed and other companies have been able to sidestep those rules by re-registering under Singaporean ownership. U.S. officials also became concerned that the firm was illegally smuggling A.I. chips into China.

A Commerce Department official visited one of the company’s data centers in Malaysia in late 2024, and found the server equipment to be packed up in boxes rather than installed, arousing suspicions about smuggling.

American and Singaporean officials met with Ms. Huang in Singapore to inquire about the company’s purchases in June of last year. Singaporean officials also detained Ms. Huang for questioning.

The Commerce Department’s work on the case was suddenly halted soon after, following an unusual interaction between Nvidia’s general counsel and a top department official.

After Singaporean officials detained Ms. Huang, Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, reached out in August to Jeff Kessler, a Commerce Department official appointed by President Trump, to ask about the detention and the case.

Mr. Teter then reached out to agents working on the Megaspeed case for information, saying that Mr. Kessler had given Nvidia permission to make the inquiries.

The incident raised questions of what Mr. Kessler and Mr. Teter had discussed, and whether those interactions could become the subject of legal proceedings. Bloomberg reported earlier that Ms. Huang’s detention was the cause of Mr. Teter’s outreach.

Commerce Department officials were subsequently told not to work on or speak about the case. In a statement this month, Singaporean officials said they had continued their work on Megaspeed, but had received limited information or assistance about the company.

Critics say the delay in imposing sanctions on Megaspeed allowed the company to continue purchasing hundreds of millions of dollars of technology. Trade data obtained from ImportGenius, a trade data platform, shows that between July 2025 and February 2026, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary received more than $800 million of shipments containing controlled Nvidia chips.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows How Nvidia’s Board Was Neutered
item.description:
Six days ago, Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia, said the chip maker’s 10-member board “does not intend to reinstate” Jensen Huang, who had resigned as chief executive after revelations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and another with a subordinate.

The board’s decision to accept Mr. Huang’s resignation was unanimous, Mr. Jones said.

But on Monday, Nvidia said that the board had “voted unanimously” to do the opposite. It was now bringing Mr. Huang back as the company’s leader. “We have every confidence in Jensen,” Mr. Jones said in a statement.

President Trump had pushed Nvidia’s board for Mr. Huang’s return, The New York Times and others reported. Mr. Trump had provided the board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges for his links with the suspected Chinese intelligence asset, who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.

Mr. Huang’s comeback — a rare reversal in corporate America over less than a week — immediately created whiplash and put a spotlight on Nvidia’s board and its decision-making. Corporate boards have a fiduciary duty to represent shareholders and guide companies to engage in best practices. But Mr. Trump effectively overrode Nvidia’s board in a campaign to reinstate Mr. Huang, exposing its weaknesses, corporate governance experts said.

“It neuters the board,” said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School and a former board member of Intel. “It makes the board look like lackeys of the president and therefore raises obvious questions of whether they really are good stewards of both the shareholders and the broader community.”

Nvidia declined to comment.

Nvidia’s board is facing particular criticism because Mr. Huang had violated the company’s code of conduct with his affairs with a subordinate and a customer, which the board now appeared to be disregarding, experts said.

Nvidia had also launched an internal investigation into Mr. Huang’s behavior and his ties with Alice Huang, a tech executive who U.S. intelligence had determined was a Chinese intelligence asset; the investigation has not concluded.

By reinstating Mr. Huang before finishing its investigation, Nvidia’s board could expose the company to shareholder lawsuits and political scrutiny over national security, said Eric Talley, a professor of corporate governance at Columbia Law School.

“They are essentially deciding they’re going to roll the dice on this and really, really hope that it doesn’t come up snake eyes,” Mr. Talley said.

In its statement on Monday, Nvidia’s board said its investigation would “proceed to conclusion,” and that “Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.” The board also said the company would hire a chief compliance officer who would report to its nominating and corporate governance committee.

Earlier this month, the board also formed a committee to oversee Nvidia’s national security policies, compliance with U.S. trade restrictions and risk management for global trade.

Nvidia’s board had a track record of loyalty and deference to Mr. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993 and built it into one of the world’s most valuable firms. Two members, Mark A. Stevens and Tench Coxe, have been on the board since 1993 after their venture capital firms invested in Nvidia. They are also among the company’s largest individual shareholders and have reaped substantial returns from their Nvidia stock.

Nvidia’s eight other board members include two former executives at a chip designer that worked with the company in the 1990s; the former chief executive of the law firm Cooley LLP, the former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs; the former chief information officer at the drugmaker Eli Lilly; the former chief marketing officer of the National Football League, the former president of Taco Bell and an engineering professor.

Before he resigned, Mr. Huang had viewed Nvidia’s board primarily as a governance requirement, rather than as an important part of the company’s strategy or execution, The Times previously reported.

Mr. Huang had flouted traditional management practices at Nvidia. He applied a flat organizational structure and had an executive staff of more than 60 people who reported to him, placing him at the center of day-to-day operations. He anointed his daughter, Madison Huang, his de facto chief of staff; and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, a leading dealmaker for the company. And Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Mr. Huang, 63.

“They gave so much of their control to him to dictate the structure of the company,” David Astorino, a senior partner at RHR International, a leadership consulting firm, said of Nvidia’s board.

After Mr. Huang resigned, his allies in Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington rallied behind him as Nvidia’s market valuation plunged by more than $1.5 trillion. The company’s share price leaped more than 30 percent on Monday after the announcement of Mr. Huang’s return.

Corporate boards have a fiduciary duty to shareholders but are “supposed to create a long-term value, not a short-term pop,” said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management.

In a statement on Monday, Mr. Huang said that he was honored to be back at Nvidia and expressed his gratitude to the board.

“I want to thank the Nvidia board for its confidence and deliberation through this process,” he said.

item.title: ‘You’re Not Dying Fast Enough’: When Medicare Hospice Caps Cut Off a Patient
item.description:
Amy Lynn Birmingham couldn’t believe she was being cut off from hospice care. Nurses who came to her home in Sandpoint, Idaho, had gotten her pain under control, managed her supply of oxygen and stabilized some symptoms from blood clots, stroke and heart failure.

But after 15 months, the for-profit hospice company in charge of her care decided last year she no longer qualified. Ms. Birmingham said a sympathetic nurse had schooled her in the reality of hospice economics: “You’re not dying fast enough.”

More than a year later, Ms. Birmingham, 64, is alive yet still dying, with a cascade of issues relating to blood clots and severe vascular disease that she is navigating outside hospice. Her case highlights what critics say are flaws in the way hospice care is delivered in the United States, a concern that is growing in urgency as boomers live longer and swell the ranks of people needing end-of-life care.

Citing fraudulent practices in the industry, the Trump administration this month extended a moratorium on new hospice agencies registering with Medicare to deliver service. But even absent wrongdoing, financial incentives frequently result in harm to patients, according to critics of the current system.

Comfort care for elderly patients and people with disabilities, typically delivered at home, has been covered by government Medicare insurance since the early 1980s. It began mostly for patients at the end of their battles with cancer. Qualifying for hospice requires a doctor to predict that a patient will die within six months.

That six-month survival benchmark influences an average per-patient cap of about $36,000 that a hospice agency can receive from Medicare, which paid an estimated $27.5 billion for end-of-life services in 2024. Patients and some experts say the cap acts as an incentive for hospice agencies to remove people who are dying on their own timetable, not the schedule baked into the regulations.

Recent evidence raises questions about whether the cap makes sense, medically or economically. Former President Jimmy Carter died in 2024 after 22 months in hospice. A study last year led by a Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist found that hospice care saved Medicare $29,000 for every patient with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia by keeping those patients out of nursing homes.

“The big picture is there is almost nothing else in health care that we can think of that makes people better off and saves money,” said the paper’s author, Jonathan Gruber, who was a central architect of a groundbreaking Massachusetts health reform that served as a model for the Affordable Care Act.

The restriction on hospice services adopted by Medicare nearly a half a century ago should be re-examined, Mr. Gruber and his colleagues wrote, because it “distorts care” and, when people are thrown off, denies vital services to people at the end of life. The researchers said their findings suggested that “expanding hospice access would reduce Medicare costs, even if it meant admitting patients who could potentially live longer than six months.”

The concept of raising or eliminating payment caps in hospice has not gained traction in Washington. Instead, hospice for years has been marked by fraud investigations, with the focal point often on whether hospice patients are truly dying. High rates of “live discharges” are a sign that hospice companies may be accepting patients who are not sick enough to qualify, according to federal officials. The number of people whose hospice care ends without their dying is rising, according to federal data — to 19 percent, or 270,000 people, in 2024 from 16 percent in 2020.

Industry representatives, while acknowledging fraud and condemning bad actors, say that hospices are balancing regulations and the threat of fines with the delicate task of estimating how long someone will live.

“It’s not an exact science,” said Patrick Harrison, vice president for policy and legislative affairs of the National Alliance for Care at Home, a trade group. “I have seen patients myself where you would not be surprised if they passed away the next day, yet they have lived for nine months or a year.”

“From a hospice perspective, there is some risk there” of having to return money to Medicare as a penalty for excessive payments, he said.

The Trump administration decided this year that hospice fraud had become such a problem that it placed a six-month moratorium on certifying new providers. This month, it extended the moratorium for another six months.

“Fraud in hospice and home health persists, and our work isn’t finished,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in announcing the extension.

The continuing moratorium drew mixed reactions from industry. “Program integrity and access to care should not be competing priorities,” said Katie Smith Sloan, president of LeadingAge, the association that represents nonprofit hospice agencies and nursing homes.

The vast majority of hospice care takes place in a person’s home, in an assisted living facility or a nursing home, according to federal data. A limited number of patients, less than 2 percent, receive care at inpatient hospice units. Four states have been targeted by various authorities as rife with hospice fraud: California, Arizona, Nevada and Texas.

A report by the state auditor in California in 2022 found high indicators of fraud in Los Angeles County, including long lengths of stay in hospice and unusually high numbers of people being discharged alive.

Hospice agencies have been accused of cherry-picking people with dementia, who live longer and require fewer nurse visits than someone dying of cancer. Legislation has been introduced in Congress that would change some of the economic incentives to better reflect the types of patients needing care.

Patient advocates point out that being discharged from hospice while alive doesn’t mean a patient isn’t dying and won’t still need help, as Ms. Birmingham learned. Patients are allowed to re-enroll with a different hospice agency, but that is not always possible in rural areas like Sandpoint with few providers.

Ms. Birmingham is a former flight engineer and aviation expert who moved from Bend, Ore., where she owned a llama ranch, to Sandpoint to be closer to her son after she had a stroke in 2022.

She was declared disabled, qualifying her for Medicare insurance, soon before she entered hospice in February 2024. Her removal from hospice, called a discharge, in May 2025 meant she was suddenly cut off from comfort care. The discharge form, which she shared with The New York Times, had a single line of justification: “Patient is no longer hospice appropriate.” She had to find a doctor in Sandpoint who would manage her complex needs, including prescribing fentanyl patches for severe pain.

“These hospice nurses cried because I got discharged,” she said. “It’s about the money.”

Auburn Crest Hospice, the for-profit provider that determined Ms. Birmingham was no longer eligible for care, did not respond to requests for comment.

Medicare reimburses hospice companies at a flat daily rate that starts above $236 for the first 60 days and then drops to $186 a day. The per-patient cap of $36,000 is applied to the average for a hospice provider’s patients.That provides an incentive for operators to remove patients from hospice once their care significantly exceeds the cap, because it will push up the company’s per-patient average and could result in financial penalties from Medicare, according to Mr. Gruber and other experts.

A study published this month in the medical journal Health Affairs found that after private equity owners purchased a for-profit hospice provider, billings increased an average of nearly 6 percent. Discharges of people who were still alive rose 11 percent.

“If a person is discharged alive from hospice, for any number of reasons, the hospice wasn’t used completely as intended,” said Dr. Sneha Kannan, an author of the analysis.

Ms. Birmingham contacted Stephanie Wladkowski, a professor at Bowling Green State University, about the cutoff to her care.

It’s disruptive for patients to be summarily removed from hospice without careful planning, said Ms. Wladkowski, who studies the effects on patients when hospice benefits end.

The problem is worse in rural areas, where patients cannot find an alternative hospice to re-enroll. Losing access to narcotic pain medications is common. So is the removal from the home of equipment, like medical-grade beds and specialized wheelchairs, Ms. Wladkowski said.

Having worked as a hospice social worker, she said she had seen how the caps influence decision-making to the detriment of patients. Hospice providers hesitate to admit some terminally ill patients, worried they will not die soon enough, she said, or they sometimes discharge someone whose decline has slowed or even reversed.

Hospice typically requires that life-saving measures be curtailed. Chemotherapy and radiation are typically stopped for cancer patients, for instance.

But palliative care continues. Debilitating pain can be reduced with the use of narcotic drugs, relieving emotional and physical stress. Insomnia, nausea and agitation can also be brought under control. Bathing, skin care and repositioning in bed reduces bed sores, infection and sepsis. Social workers and chaplains offer counseling.

There is some evidence those measures prolong life for patients with certain diseases, including congestive heart failure and lung cancer.

Ms. Birmingham believes hospice extended her life. Since she was dropped from hospice in May 2025, she has been paying out of her own pocket for in-home care because she realized the benefit to her well-being.

“Imagine my surprise when I lasted,” she said. “And here I am, still.”

item.title: From Chinese Factory Town to the Nvidia Scandal: The Rise of Alice Huang
item.description:
The rows of matching yellow apartment blocks are each four stories tall and bear a name from another era: Patriotic Village No. 5.

One of the weathered apartments belonged to the family of Alice Huang, whose father worked as a clerk at a sprawling complex of weapons factories in Nanzhushan, a village nestled in the hills of southern China’s Hunan Province.

The complex had a number too: State-Owned Factory No. 282. It made everything from hand grenades to parts for guided missiles, and under China’s Soviet-style planned economy, life in the area revolved around it.

Today, the town is well past its prime. The factory complex remains, but after state-owned enterprise layoffs, many young people started moving away. By the mid-2000s, one of them was Ms. Huang, who rose from this fading industrial town to the inner circle of the man behind America’s artificial intelligence boom — and into the middle of a geopolitical crisis.

The New York Times traced Ms. Huang’s life through visits to Nanzhushan village and four countries, drawing on internal company documents, corporate filings and interviews with more than a dozen people familiar with her. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

The reporting reveals previously unreported details of her upbringing, education and business dealings that show how Ms. Huang’s life has been intertwined with China’s military-industrial complex since childhood.

U.S. intelligence officials believe Ms. Huang was in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 through this year. That period overlapped with at least part of the time she allegedly had an affair with Jensen Huang, the chief executive of American chip giant Nvidia. It also coincided with large purchases of Nvidia’s advanced chips by her company Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence agencies have also gathered evidence that her business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency.

Those contacts led some U.S. officials to suspect that Mr. Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Nov. 12, had been targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation, which Beijing denies. The case heightened concerns in Washington about Beijing’s efforts to acquire advanced American chips and accelerate its A.I. ambitions.

The claims about Ms. Huang continue to reverberate. On Monday, in a stunning turnabout, Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated Mr. Huang as C.E.O. after pressure from President Trump. Despite the president’s support, Mr. Huang and his ties to Ms. Huang are expected to be scrutinized in Congress next week, when he is set to appear before three committees.

Since childhood, her life was surrounded by China’s defense establishment. She attended a school for children of workers at a weapons factory owned by a state-run company repeatedly sanctioned by the U.S. government.

Ms. Huang had established her own ties to the Chinese government by the time she was an adult. She worked briefly for China’s state broadcaster and later made an investment that would connect her to the son of a former Chinese vice premier. As an entrepreneur, she remained within the state’s orbit, securing backing and funding from local government officials for a business that served Beijing’s strategic imperatives.

Through a web of family and business relationships that gave her access to Nvidia chips, she is linked to Chinese state-owned defense contractors that supply the People’s Liberation Army.

The story of a factory worker’s daughter from rural China who found herself at the center of a global struggle over technology and espionage is one of ambition, reinvention and China’s rise from a drab socialist state to a shiny world power.

Alice Huang grew up in the shadow of Mao Zedong, whose birthplace is just a 20-minute drive away. Her father worked at the local plant, part of Jiangnan Industries Group, a subsidiary of the military supplier Norinco.

She attended local schools, where she was a good student but not at the top of her class, according to the neighborhood committee cadre. She later enrolled in a nursing school in the nearby city of Xiangtan, according to a current student named Joanna, who said a teacher had described Alice Huang as a graduate.

After graduating, Ms. Huang, who turns 44 next month, did what tens of millions of Chinese in her generation did. She left small-town life for better opportunities in bigger cities like Beijing and Shanghai.

Over two decades, she became a globe-trotting executive overseeing Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s advanced chips.

Yet traces of her early life proved difficult to pin down. Villagers gossiped about the family, whom some remembered, but none could identify the precise house where she grew up. Local officials disagreed about her mother’s background.

Two Times journalists interviewed village leaders and several residents before the police halted their reporting and took them to the nearest police station for questioning.

By her 20s, Alice Huang had left Nanzhushan. She worked for state television at the flagship channel of China’s state broadcaster, according to an online résumé and a former classmate.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

She attended Hong Kong Baptist University in 2006 to pursue a master’s degree in media management. The program was new and drew many students from mainland China, who, one former professor recalled, were often there for reasons beyond education. Hong Kong was a gateway to the world, with open internet and easy travel.

A classmate said she often wore designer brands, a contrast with the jeans and T-shirts most other students wore. She often skipped classes, the person said, and many students suspected that connections in China kept her in the school.

In 2010, she and her older sister, Huang Yu, registered a company at the address of a building inside a members-only golf course in Beijing. Their father, Huang Guobin, by then of retirement age, was listed as a company supervisor in Chinese corporate records.

The golf course was a magnet for government officials and the businessmen who courted them. Its restaurant served shark fin, and its chef had worked at the walled compound where Chinese leaders host heads of state, according to Chinese media reports. A senior civil-aviation official was once punished for accepting more than 50 free rounds of golf there.

It is unclear what the Huang family business did. It reported taking in only about $4,500 in 2012. In 2014, Alice transferred her stake to her sister.

Soon, the Huang sisters moved on to far larger ventures.

Alice Huang’s hometown Nanzhushan sits next to the G60 expressway. Follow it some 700 miles to the northeast and it ends in Shanghai, passing in its final miles by a cluster of giant data centers in the city’s Songjiang District.

There, she made her mark with a sprawling data center featuring advanced American A.I. chips. The project also brought her into the orbit of Nvidia’s Mr. Huang.

Alice Huang was in Shanghai by the mid-2010s. In meetings, she introduced a well-known financier, Kang Wei, as her husband. Together, they invested in a network of companies with overlapping ownership, shareholders and contact information, according to corporate filings and records from WireScreen, a data platform.

She put her money alongside some of China’s most sophisticated and politically connected financiers. At one point, she used a Caribbean shell company to invest in a Chinese medical device maker before its public share sale, according to a filing with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Among the other investors was a fund founded by the son of Liu He, who was then a vice premier of China and a member of the Communist Party’s ruling Politburo.

Alice Huang initially owned a key holding company for the network. In 2017, as with the golf company, she transferred her stake to her older sister.

During Covid, Alice Huang and Mr. Kang helped develop a data center with local government support — a project that made her a potentially useful contact for State Security. When it was finished, the project, called the Yangtze River Delta A.I. Advanced Computing Center, featured Nvidia chips and leased computing power to companies.

The data center and a company set up to acquire Nvidia servers and rent out computing power, called Century Litong, soon became a key link in a chip supply pipeline. The flows traveled into a network of companies linked to Chinese military contractors like the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, China’s state aerospace and defense conglomerate, and an A.I. lab linked to the People’s Liberation Army.

As borders reopened after the pandemic, the couple looked abroad. In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team had introduced Alice Huang to the Chinese technology giant Alibaba. She and Mr. Kang began pitching investors on a venture to buy Nvidia chips, install them in Southeast Asia and sell the A.I. computing power to Chinese companies.

In 2023, Alice Huang used a British Virgin Islands company to buy a Singaporean subsidiary of 7Road, a gaming company. It became Megaspeed.

The U.S. government had begun tightening restrictions on sales of advanced A.I. chips to China, prompting companies to eliminate ties to the mainland. Alice Huang began cultivating an image as an international executive. She posted pictures of herself drinking wine at fine restaurants across Asia alongside Nvidia’s Mr. Huang and tycoons from the region’s chip and electronics supply chain.

To those around them, their China connections were obvious. In one pitch deck from 2025, their data center business heralded computing centers operating in Shanghai, Shenzhen, Anhui, Sichuan, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia — a mix of locations that tied a data center network in China to one in Southeast Asia, where the most advanced Nvidia chips could be bought.

Although the relationship with Mr. Huang was not yet public, U.S. intelligence agencies had identified Alice Huang as an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. By the fall of 2025, President Trump had been briefed on the intelligence.

Alice Huang’s newfound prominence has reached Nanzhushan.

One store manager said locals had been discussing the news quietly. Although coverage has not been widely censored, the subject remains sensitive.

In Patriotic Village No. 5, people were less cautious.

“We are all gossiping about it,” admitted a neighbor surnamed Zheng, who once made hand grenades at the factory. Another resident said many had been discussing her looks.

In nearby Xiangtan, a man surnamed Han said he looked up to Alice Huang. Times have been tough, and it was becoming harder for local people to make money, he said. That a homegrown person could get rich was impressive.

“I don’t care if she is the mistress of Jensen Huang,” he said. “She is great because she is a successful businesswoman.”

Alexandra Stevenson, Selam Gebrekidan, Murphy Zhao and Anjali Tsui contributed reporting from Hong Kong. Xinyun Wu and Pei-Lin Wu contributed reporting from Taipei. Ruoxin Zhang contributed research.

item.title: You Can Call Restaurants Again. A Human Might Even Answer.
item.description:
In 2012, my first year as restaurant critic for The Times, I published the telephone number of almost every place I reviewed. By the time I left the job, in 2024, I no longer asked, “What’s your number?” The relevant question by then was: “Do you have a phone?”

Very often, the answer was no. Most people reserve online now, I was told, and the staff is too busy to answer the phone.

Calling restaurants for reservations — indeed, calling restaurants for anything at all — seemed to be on the way to the hospitality graveyard, to be laid to rest alongside smoking sections and ladies’ menus, which discreetly omitted all prices so a woman never needed to know how much her male date was forking over for her blanquette de veau.

But a funny thing happened on the way to the graveyard. Diners didn’t stop picking up the phone. And now a number of start-ups are vying for the privilege of answering their calls. The voice on the other end of the line may not be human, but we’ll get to that in a minute.

Inside a small office in SoHo, flesh-and-blood employees of a year-old business called Broome Street Concierge field calls, texts and emails from diners and would-be diners on behalf of six restaurants. The operators have the same access to the reservations platforms as an on-site host. They know which two-tops can be pushed together and how many seats the owners hope to fill, or leave empty, each night. (New restaurants often run below capacity while they work out the kinks.)

They have other answers at their fingertips, too, about things like wheelchair access, allergens and the odds of barging in on the spur of the moment and getting a table.

The office also secures tables, even when there appear to be none online, for investors, celebrities, in-laws, big spenders and anyone else to whom the restaurants have slipped a separate, text-only number. Many people who run new or perennially jammed establishments say they are now besieged by such special pleadings. An owner of one downtown restaurant, speaking for a good part of the industry, told a reporter for Eater in 2023, “All I do is filter the DM requests. It’s nonstop.”

The messages rain down so hard these days that Andrea Czachor, the founder of Broome Street Concierge, has made it part of her sales pitch.

“One thing I’m saying to owners is: People, how much longer do you want to be attached to your phone like this?” she said. “Can you turn your phone over for two and a half hours while you’re having dinner?”

Broome Street Concierge handles calls for Estela and Altro Paradiso in Manhattan — Ms. Czachor is president of the group that owns both — and four other restaurants she won’t name. She says they requested not to be identified, so diners can believe that their questions are being fielded by the establishments’ own employees.

“One of the things the clients are really proud of is that no one knows it’s not their internal team,” Ms. Czachor said.

For restaurants that aren’t quite as particular about the illusion they create, at least a dozen tech firms will provide many of the same services using a bot that runs on artificial intelligence. The voices sound almost human, although, like other chatbots, A.I. reservationists may give themselves away with unnaturally long pauses or by stumbling over vague, confusing requests.

Early this year a Reddit user posted a video of an A.I. agent for a San Francisco wine bar that seemed to have a nervous breakdown, emitting a single, prolonged, drone-like vowel after it was asked whether any tables were available at the moment.

On the other hand, these A.I. operators don’t sleep, get the flu or show up to work with a hangover. They can handle more than one call at a time, and will pick up the phone around the clock, every bit as calm and patient at midnight as they are during the dinner rush.

Some bots have other tricks up their digital sleeves. Bitebuddy, designed for Mexican restaurants, will take reservations in English or Spanish. Superhost, in use at a number of national restaurant groups including Carmine’s and Legal Sea Foods, speaks 97 languages. Another bot, Hostie, has a theatrical bent. At the garlic-crazy restaurant the Stinking Rose, the Hostie operator introduces himself as Vladimir in deep, Transylvanian cadences.

Most of these services got off the ground within the past two or three years. They are in hot competition for a market that has turned out to be very receptive to their pitches, as restaurants struggle to rein in rising costs, including the higher wages that have come along with a labor shortage in the industry.

Any ringing phone that goes unanswered may be a missed opportunity to win or keep a customer. Besides the hard math of getting rumps in chairs, reservationists can exert a form of soft power, making diners feel good about the prospect of a meal they are going to eat days or months in the future.

“Hospitality really begins before the guest even arrives,” said E.J. Lagasse, the chef of Emeril’s in New Orleans. Telephones never went out of style at Emeril’s, founded in 1990 by Mr. Lagasse’s father, Emeril. (Yes, that Emeril.) Three living, breathing reservationists work full time inside a small room inside the restaurant, booking tables for the 20 percent or so of customers who don’t use Resy.

Because not all old-time fans know that after he took over the kitchen, E.J. Lagasse instituted a tasting menu, the reservationists make sure they’re up to date. Those who are hungry for classic Emeril’s dishes might be steered toward a reservation next door at the Wine Bar at Emeril’s, where gumbo and barbecue shrimp are still served. The office also alerts the chef when a repeat customer is coming, a longstanding tradition at Emeril’s.

“Dad was always super-big on knowing who was in the restaurant,” Mr. Lagasse said. Because New Orleans isn’t “a super-mega-metropolis,” he said, locals can quickly become regulars.

The soft power of hospitality runs best on firm guidelines. The 15 or so employees in the reservations office of the Keith McNally Restaurant Group on lower Broadway, around the corner from Balthazar, are instructed in a number of rules. Smile when you’re talking on the phone. Don’t correct a customer. Never say “no problem.” Never say “no,” for that matter.

“We always offer another possibility instead,” said Roberta Delice, the group’s director of operations. “Another rule is that you can always break a rule to make a customer happy.”

Unfortunately, you can’t make everybody happy. The writer Foster Kamer, who manned phones in the McNally boiler room two decades ago, remembers the job as “soul-sucking” because it often required disappointing people who were used to getting exactly what they want.

“Many people would immediately just get so huffy and angry, and jump from ‘I want this thing’ to ‘I am mad at you, the person telling me I can’t have it,’” Mr. Kamer said.

An abused reservationist is not necessarily inclined to work miracles for his abuser. But, Mr. Kamer said, “if somebody was nice and you heard something in their voice that was genuine,” he would go out of his way to squeeze them in. His favorite part of the job, he said, was “saying yes to people who just earnestly wanted to be there.”

Perhaps a chatbot can be tuned to recognize the sounds of human decency if it is fed enough examples of living people talking with other living people. But for now, humans probably have a more nuanced feel for the art of hospitality.

At Eulalie, a restaurant in TriBeCa, the only way to get a table is to talk to Tina Vaughn, one of the owners. She writes each day’s reservations on the left side of a leather-bound date book. On the right side, she sketches a seating chart and jots down special requests, allergies, favorite wines and other quirks. The books become records of who has been to Eulalie and what happened while they were there.

The other week, a computer science professor came in. When he said that algorithms are his specialty, Ms. Vaughn showed him her reservations book.

“This is my algorithm,” she said.

item.title: Top Aviation Officials Were Traveling When Flights Were Halted Nationwide
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands of travelers were hobbled when the Federal Aviation Administration called a halt to flights nationwide on Nov. 13.

Among those caught up in the stoppage — either in the air at the time or having just flown — were top transportation officials and contractors involved in addressing the problem.

The fact that they, too, were in transit highlighted what everyone learned firsthand that Friday: busy weekend travel days can be a bad time try to fix aging aviation technology.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who oversees the F.A.A., was himself mid-flight, en route to Washington after visiting vendor facilities in Texas.

“I was on the airplane, an airplane from Dallas when this happened, hence my attire, and haven’t gone to change, so I apologize for wearing a jacket and jeans with you,” Mr. Duffy said during a White House news conference later that day.

Mr. Duffy has been pushing through air-traffic control upgrades at a speedy pace to complete them by the end of President Trump’s term. The F.A.A., under Mr. Duffy’s watch, has come under criticism for authorizing the work that led to the stop in the middle of a Friday, a time of week when air travel typically spikes.

Aviation experts previously told The New York Times that such upgrades had historically been performed overnight or during midday periods when fewer planes are flying — and not on Fridays — in case something goes wrong.

And something went seriously wrong on that Friday, Nov. 13.

The F.A.A. has still not announced the exact cause of the technical disruption that led to the longest stop of United States air travel since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. But officials have suggested it happened after a technician for L3Harris Technologies, a contractor working on the modernization project, installed a new router at an F.A.A. facility in El Dorado, Ark.

What was supposed to be a single, routine upgrade somehow stymied the nation’s air traffic control system.

The situation, which caused the cancellation of thousands of flights and disruptions that extended throughout the weekend, has prompted finger pointing between transportation officials and the vendor about who was to blame for the initial problem and whether it was remedied quickly enough.

Officials at the F.A.A. have questioned the staffing levels at L3Harris’s Melbourne, Fla., headquarters and requested a list of employees who were physically present at the facility during the incident, according to four people familiar with their correspondence who requested anonymity to discuss internal matters. L3Harris sent them staffing information in response.

In a statement, L3Harris said that it had been fully staffed that day and had responded quickly and appropriately to the F.A.A. to help resolve the issue.

While many important details of the events of that day are still not known, the following is an account of what transpired immediately after the F.A.A. realized it might have an issue on that frantic Friday.

L3Harris, a large defense contractor, is responsible for maintaining the networks that facilitate communications between air traffic controllers and pilots. Many parts of the nation’s air traffic control system are obsolete, and the company is in the midst of upgrading copper wire to high-speed fiber optic cable.

Shortly after completing about five hours of work that day, the L3Harris technician in El Dorado who was installing the router noticed a problem, said two people familiar with the matter.

Because the L3Harris employee had been approved to do the work at the facility and an F.A.A. official on site was not expected to provide detailed supervision of the job, the L3Harris worker called his company’s headquarters in Florida to request assistance, those people added.

Kaitlyn Arena, a spokeswoman for L3Harris, said that the F.A.A. had approved the timing of the work at El Dorado after conducting its own operational risk assessment.

As the technician was reaching out to L3Harris’s headquarters around 3 p.m. Eastern time, the F.A.A.’s air traffic command center in Warrenton, Va., detected that its communication system was being overloaded.

The F.A.A. feared the glitch meant that air traffic controllers could not effectively guide pilots while they were flying, though in the end officials never completely lost communication and the systems outages, while widespread, did not engulf the entire system.

Leaders at the command center in Warrenton called an emergency meeting with top officials at the F.A.A., including Bryan Bedford, its administrator, and Franklin J. McIntosh, who runs the agency’s air traffic control division.

Mr. Bedford and Mr. McIntosh had just completed their own weekend travel to their respective homes in Indiana and Texas, said three people with knowledge of their movements who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The leaders also reached out to Mr. Duffy, who was in the air.

From their respective locations, Mr. Duffy, Mr. Bedford and Mr. McIntosh participated in an initial emergency call at 3:45 p.m. with leaders at the command center, minutes after controllers there noticed the widening problem.

During that virtual meeting, the Warrenton officials explained the situation and their determination that a nationwide flight stoppage had to be issued to protect passengers and crews — an assessment with which Mr. Bedford and Mr. Duffy agreed, according to two transportation officials.

The nationwide halt was enacted at 3:54 p.m. Planes continued to land but new flights could not take off. Airlines’ call centers were quickly flooded with desperate customers, trying to rebook.

L3Harris was not involved in the decision to halt flights but was quickly brought into discussions to resolve the situation.

Coincidentally, two senior L3Harris executives on the F.A.A. contract were also in the air at that time.

Kathy Crandall, president of the company’s mission networks division, and Chris Collings, the vice president and general manager of managed services, were both on long-haul flights back to the United States from a business trip in Australia, said people with knowledge of their movements who requested anonymity to discuss confidential matters.

They joined calls with F.A.A. officials when they landed.

Ms. Arena, in the statement, declined to discuss the executives by name, but said that the F.A.A. had reached a L3Harris senior leader with decision-making authority “immediately” by phone and another joined a call with the F.A.A. within a minute of receiving an invite.

Isolating the source of the problem in order to get planes back in the air safely was a prolonged process among government officials and L3Harris employees. Officials from both the F.A.A. and L3Harris say their staffing was sufficient to tackle the problem, even though it took several hours to resolve.

L3Harris officials said that their network operations center — a round-the-clock monitoring facility the company operates in Melbourne — was at full strength.

Senior company executives — including the chief executive, Sam Mehta — were at the network operations center in Melbourne “immediately after being notified of the issue,” Ms. Arena said.

The company also brought in additional workers to help manage the situation, two people with knowledge of what happened said.

Over the next few hours, officials managed to identify and isolate two facilities in Arkansas and Texas that had been overloading the network and disable the misconfigured routers, allowing them to bring the air traffic network back online, F.A.A. leaders told reporters.

At 8:15 p.m., the ground stop lifted, and flights began to take off again.

Kate, Nick and Karoun dug into how Nov. 13 turned from a routine travel day for hundreds of thousands of people to an utter mess. We all learned first hand how Fridays can be a bad day to try to upgrade aging aviation technology.
