item.title: Young New Yorkers Are Losing on Kalshi, City Council Says
item.description:
The youngest users of the prediction market site Kalshi in New York City are losing money at a disproportionate rate, according to findings released on Tuesday by the City Council.

In one of the first investigations by a local government into the users of prediction markets, the City Council found that people aged 18 to 20 years old represented about one-tenth of New York City accounts on Kalshi in the first 10 months of the year. But those users accounted for one-sixth of all losses from individual people in the city, or about $8.9 million.

In total, individuals in New York City lost more than they won, with a net loss of more than $52 million during that time frame. On the other hand, institutional traders in the city, meaning businesses or funds, made a net gain of more than $340 million, the City Council said.

The report represented the preliminary findings of an investigation started earlier this year. The city also requested information from other platforms, including Polymarket, Coinbase and Gemini Titan. A final report will be released in December.

“Nearly 500,000 individual Kalshi accounts are registered to a New York City address, with net losses totaling millions of dollars,” Julie Menin, the City Council speaker, said in a statement. “The disproportionate financial and mental tolls on young New Yorkers are simply unacceptable.”

Of the nearly half a million Kalshi accounts in New York City, around 27 percent belonged to users under the age of 25, the report found.

A spokeswoman for Kalshi, Dani Lever, said the City Council’s initial findings lacked context, making “this snapshot of data misleading.” She said any individual trading through a limited liability corporation counts as an institution, and the average monthly loss for 18- to 20-year-olds in New York was only $17.40.

“A fair market isn’t about equal outcomes. It’s about equal opportunities. As in options and futures, skill matters,” she said.

Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket have exploded in popularity this year, particularly with younger people. The companies have drawn tens of billions of dollars in wagers on topics from sports to elections, but their popularity has also drawn concerns about whether they violate state gambling laws, and can be manipulated by people with insider information.

The city’s report could add to growing calls to restrict prediction markets only to those 21 and older. The platforms are largely available to users 18 and up across the United States.

Experts argue that prediction markets have effectively lowered the age of online gambling, which most states limit to people 21 and older, and have raised concerns about the susceptibility of young adults to gambling addiction. The companies argue that their sites do not offer gambling, rather a financial tool for hedging risk. Gambling addiction experts often say that prediction markets offer the same experience as gambling.

The concerns have led at least a dozen states to sue the platforms, including New York, whose attorney general sued Kalshi in July, accusing the company of operating illegally and in defiance of state gambling laws.

In a hearing on the state’s case at New York County Supreme Court on Monday, Justice Melissa Crane denied the state’s request to temporarily block the company’s operations. But she said she was “very concerned” about Kalshi being available to “kids” aged 18 to 20 and asked the parties “to discuss a way of safeguarding for that age group” within the week.

The City Council, where some members have said they would support legislation to restrict access to prediction market sites, has scheduled a hearing next month and will invite executives from all of the companies to testify.

Late last month, Kalshi introduced default $2,500 monthly deposit limits for accounts for 18- to 20-year-olds.

The City Council announced the investigation into major prediction market platforms in August. The council said it would focus on whether the companies had used false or deceptive marketing, with particular concern for content directed toward young people, and sought to determine whether the industry needs additional consumer protections.

item.title: How Huang’s Return Rewrote Corporate America’s Rules
item.description:
Andrew here. Why did President Trump want Jensen Huang back so badly? The conventional wisdom would cite the market sell-off and Trump’s interest in helping prop up the A.I. industry. But there may be a more personal reason.

Look at the altered image of Huang posted to Trump’s social media account on Monday. It closely resembles a picture taken from the 2024 assassination attempt on Trump in Butler, Pa. — with the Nvidia chief in his place. On CNBC on Monday, Trump said more than once that Huang “went through hell.” And the president has long portrayed efforts to prosecute him as politically motivated. I suspect he sees some of himself in Huang.

Trump has also now made the phrase “too big to fail” — historically applied to institutions — apply to an individual as well.

But he may also have made Nvidia one of the biggest targets of Congress, even as Huang is set to testify on Capitol Hill next week. How did restricted Nvidia chips get to China? What did company executives know? What did the White House tell the board about reinstalling Huang? These are questions that some Republicans have, sure — but expect Democrats to go after every email, text message and intelligence assessment related to Nvidia when they assume power in January.

All of this makes me think about Jamie Dimon and JPMorgan Chase’s 2008 takeover of Bear Stearns at Washington’s behest. Dimon assumed the government wouldn’t go after his bank for Bear Stearns’s mortgage transgressions — only for JPMorgan to eventually agree to a $13 billion settlement of the matter. “We would not do something like Bear Stearns again,” Dimon has said since. “In fact, I don’t think our board would let me take the call.”

But, it appears, memories are short.

Jensen Huang is back in the saddle at Nvidia, to the satisfaction of President Trump, several top tech moguls and financiers and stock market investors.

But how Huang came back has raised questions about the future of the world’s most prominent chip maker, the artificial intelligence trade — and, perhaps, American-style free-market capitalism.

“Did I do a good job last night?” Trump told The Times on Monday, essentially confirming that he played a major role in the reinstatement of Huang. The Times adds that Trump asked Vice President JD Vance, a former venture capitalist, to help make it happen, including by giving the Nvidia board assurances that Huang posed no national security threat and wasn’t facing criminal charges. Trump also told news outlets that he spoke with the board.

Secrecy was paramount: Only a few administration officials and Nvidia executives (a group that reportedly didn’t include Colette Kress, then the company’s interim C.E.O.) knew about the discussions.

It was Trump’s biggest intervention yet in a private company, in a second term in which he has already sought to reshape corporate policies like eliminating diversity initiatives and changing pricing practices, and demanded a 10 percent stake in Intel.

Trump has long viewed the stock market as a proxy for the U.S. economy and Nvidia as a national A.I. champion worth protecting. But actually leaning on the chip maker’s board to reinstall Huang — and essentially indemnifying directors for doing so — was extraordinary by many experts’ reckoning. Jeffrey Gordon, a professor at Columbia Law School, told DealBook that it was an example of what he called “presidentialism.”

It won’t be smooth sailing for Huang. While his return added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia’s market value on Monday, fundamental questions about competition in the A.I. chip market and the fundamentals of the industry’s growth prospects still remain. (More on that below.)

The Nvidia chief is scheduled to testify before Congress — including in a public hearing — next week. And both Democrats and Republicans professed incredulity and anger at both Huang’s return and how it came about:

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing,” Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, wrote on social media.

Huang’s return “only increases the urgency to pass bipartisan export control bills” for A.I. chips, wrote Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, who is set to be chair of the Senate Banking Committee in January.

Huang’s behavior “does not support reinstatement,” wrote Senator Pete Ricketts, Republican of Nebraska, adding that he wanted to keep investigating Nvidia and Huang.

What else? We have some questions:

The Nvidia board said it “unanimously” voted to reinstate Huang. But in light of its about-face from two weeks ago — a reversal that Bernstein analysts called “clown-like” — will any members resign?

Many Nvidia employees professed relief that Huang had returned to the company. But given reports of his often abrasive management style and questions about Nvidia’s corporate governance (more on that below) will others seek to leave?

Given Trump’s willingness to rewrite traditional government-company relations, how will other corporate leaders respond?

Kalshi says it’s open to banning users under 21. The prediction market Kalshi told a New York State judge on Monday that it was willing to negotiate on the issue during a hearing about the state’s effort to crack down on the platform. The judge declined New York’s request for a temporary ban on Kalshi there, but told the sides to reach a deal by Monday. Separately, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah amid the state’s criminal case against the company and its founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara.

Are more interest rate increases in the cards? The president of the New York Fed, John Williams, suggested on Monday that the central bank would have to continue raising rates to bring inflation down, adding to a recent chorus of hawkish calls by policymakers. The comments come before the release on Wednesday of the Personal Consumption Expenditures report, which is expected to show continued growth in consumer spending last month. The futures market this morning sees two rate increases by March.

Prosecutors detail the case against a former OpenAI engineer. The engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, captured recordings of dozens of internal company meetings, including at least one between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government, federal prosecutors said in a court filing. Alfozan, who was arrested last month and accused of planting a recording device in OpenAI offices, has asked to be released before trial, a request prosecutors have opposed.

The Nvidia rally is already losing steam, a potential new worry for investors who already doubt the durability of the artificial intelligence boom.

Some bulls may look to the $3 trillion rally on Monday as a sign that the A.I. investment spigot will stay on now that the industry’s biggest champion, Jensen Huang, is back in charge at Nvidia. But for bears, the pullback this morning is a reminder that the A.I. buildout faces a host of challenges that an individual alone can’t quickly fix, Bernhard Warner writes.

The latest:

Sinking tech stocks are dragging S&P 500 futures into the red. On Monday, the benchmark index jumped 4.7 percent, its best single-day rally since April 2025 when President Trump postponed some of his most bruising tariffs.

Shares of Nvidia are down more than 5 percent, after they posted an astonishing 31.5 percent gain on Monday, their best one-day performance since 2003. (The chip maker’s stock is still down more than 30 percent from its Oct. 6 closing price.)

Was Monday’s rally a mirage? Huang may be back, but concerns about A.I. financing, the uncertain economics of commercializing the technology and the political resistance to data centers haven’t gone away.

Adam Turnquist, the chief technical strategist at LPL Financial, said the huge market gains on Monday were “an overreaction.” But so, too, was the sell-off last week, he told DealBook.

There is some grist for the bulls: Many analysts, Turnquist noted, still forecast A.I. capital expenditures of at least $1 trillion next year.

“That’s a pretty good tailwind,” he said, “not only just for the A.I. ecosystem, but for earnings, for the economy.”

Others see something more ominous in Huang’s return. Trump has taken credit for the board’s decision to bring back Huang. Even for a president who has shown a willingness to blur the lines between politics and business, the ramifications of his latest corporate intervention could rattle markets.

“Investors must reassess the risk of political involvement in U.S. corporate affairs,” Paul Donovan, the chief economist for UBS Global Wealth Management, wrote to investors this morning.

Picture of the day

Few people seemed happier about Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as C.E.O. of Nvidia than President Trump. In an interview with The Times on Monday, the president seemed to take credit for the move. He also rejoiced on social media in multiple posts, including with a meme that depicted a triumphant but bloodied Huang holding aloft a red bra.

Huang appears to have been swapped in for the president in a famous picture that showed Trump soon after he survived an assassination attempt at a campaign rally in Butler, Pa., in 2024.

Nvidia filled one job on Monday. It also began a search for another.

The chip giant said that it was planning to hire the company’s first chief compliance officer, in light of the independent investigation into how Nvidia processors ended up in China despite U.S. restrictions.

The job is a sign of changing corporate governance at Nvidia — but comes despite much bigger challenges at a company that reinstated Jensen Huang after pressure by President Trump, Sri Muppidi reports.

What’s changing: Until now, the company spread responsibility for compliance across senior management, including Huang and other senior managers, according to a regulatory filing.

Nvidia is likely to look at external candidates, according to Ash Athawale, a senior vice president of executive search at Robert Half, a global staffing company.

That’s on top of the board forming a national security and export control committee, composed of independent directors to oversee “trade compliance and national security risks.”

It’s late in coming, according to some experts. “The board is putting in place processes it should have had years ago,” Ann Lipton, a professor of corporate governance at the University of Colorado Boulder, told DealBook.

But, she added, “Huang is the one running the show and the compliance hire will have as much teeth as Huang allows.”

The bigger concern is Nvidia’s overall corporate governance, others say. The Huang scandal cast a spotlight on what experts said was a notably weak board, largely deferential to its C.E.O. And while Nvidia’s code of conduct urges employees to “avoid situations where our actions might create a conflict,” including personal relationships, Huang confessed to an affair with a customer — and reportedly admitted to more affairs over the weekend, according to The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed sources.

How he was rehired, and that it comes amid an independent inquiry by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, raises bigger issues:

Huang’s return raises questions about whether the board’s members really are good stewards of both the shareholders and the broader community,” David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School and a former board member of Intel, told The Times.

It would have been preferable to wait until Wachtell’s inquiry was finished, Larry Cunningham, the presiding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, told DealBook.

What next? Given Trump’s insistence on the importance of Huang, and the president’s role in helping reinstate him, it’s unclear how the board would hold its C.E.O. accountable in the future.

Deals

Sanofi has agreed to buy Insmed, a U.S. maker of drugs for respiratory illnesses, for $41 billion in cash, in what is seen as the biggest M.&A. deal in the industry this year. (WSJ)

Sierra, a company the former Salesforce co-C.E.O. Bret Taylor helped found that assists businesses with the building of artificial intelligence agents, said it had raised $1.75 billion at a valuation of $30 billion. Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners led the round. (Bloomberg)

Politics, policy and regulation

Oregon and Virginia sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX over Grok Imagine, an A.I. tool that has allowed users to create sexualized images of women and children. (NYT)

A Senate panel is reportedly investigating whether Vice President JD Vance played a role in the awarding of a major Venezuelan oil contract tied to one of his political donors. (Reuters)

Best of the rest

“She Was the Model Female Entrepreneur. Then the F.B.I. Knocked at Her Door.” (NYT)

“Oklahoma!” Some conservatives who fled Democratic-led states for Texas before it turned blue may now be looking north. (WSJ)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: It’s Always Black Friday Somewhere
item.description:
In some cases, the emails hit shoppers’ inboxes as early as Nov. 2: “Black Friday starts now.”

They came from brands like Glossier, AG1 and Net-a-Porter, offering discounts on makeup, supplements, luxury clothing and home goods.

If it seems as if the sales are starting earlier and dragging on forever, it’s because they are.

Black Friday shopping is no longer reserved for the day after Thanksgiving. It has taken over the entire month of November, as brands push their sales earlier. This year, 64 percent of luxury and premium brands ran sales in the first 11 days of November, up from 57 percent last year, according to data from Edited, a retail analytics firm.

One reason for the extended shopping period is that brands want to capture customers’ attention before they spend their money elsewhere later in the month, said Krista Corrigan, a senior retail analyst at Edited.

But because the sales run for longer, in order to protect their profits, brands are not able to offer appealing discounts. Gone (mostly) are the days of 70 and 80 percent doorbusters. More common lately are 20 percent off markdowns or sales of “up to” 60 percent off, where just a few items meet that upper threshold.

“There is a bit of a distrust when it comes to consumers with Black Friday,” Corrigan said. “You’re trying to decipher, am I really getting a deal? Or did this retailer bring in something, double the price and then tell me it’s 50 percent off?”

Many shoppers are feeling “Black Friday fatigue,” she added.

That may be why some brands have dropped the term “Black Friday” altogether. Luxury labels like the Row, Phoebe Philo and Toteme as well as mass brands like H&M and Aritzia have instead described their November sales as “private,” “early access” or for “members only,” lending a sense of exclusivity to a sale season that can be considered a bit garish.

Thirdlove, which sells underwear and pajamas, still refers to its deals as a Black Friday sale, even though it starts in mid-November. Heidi Zak, the brand’s founder and chief executive, has found that if “Black Friday” is omitted from promotional materials, customers “think that there’s another, better deal coming.” The move, Zak said, is meant to motivate them to shop early.

Many shoppers are aware of the tactics meant to play on their desires.

Earlier this month, Chelsey Ramlochan signed up for a private sale hosted by Swt Active, an Australian active-wear brand. Ramlochan, 33, a marketing manager in Los Angeles, had regularly shopped from the company over the years.

Looking at her cart, Ramlochan noticed that the price for the leggings she wanted appeared to have risen and that the sale price was now more than the garment’s original price.

Dean Bader, Swt Active’s director and chief financial officer said the brand did not inflate its prices ahead of its sale, describing the discounts as “genuine.” (The brand’s website experienced technical difficulties during the sale which led to American shoppers seeing the price of their assortment in Australian dollars, Bader said.)

“I ended up not even shopping. I’m very petty, so I unsubscribed from their email list,” she said, adding that the prices she had seen this season had “gotten out of control.”

Shoppers are especially sensitive to shallow discounts this Black Friday as they feel squeezed by increases in the cost of living. Femi Folarin, a clinical trial associate in New Jersey, said that this year she was refraining from buying a new luxury blow dryer, opting instead to repurchase staples in her beauty routine.

“Instead of buying wants, I’m just buying my needs,” Folarin, 25, said.

It’s not the Black Friday of her childhood. She remembered her parents “mapping out what their shopping route was going to be and how they would be able to hit all the stores,” she said.

“The sales were so good,” she said, that one year, her family ventured to Best Buy to secure a flat screen television. This year, she has opted to stay away from most Black Friday deals, which she described as “underwhelming.”

Many brands seem to have sales and promotions running almost constantly, like a 20 percent coupon for signing up for email marketing. Those have trained many shoppers to expect even bigger discounts on Black Friday — or to feel more than fine letting Black Friday blow past them.

“It’s just sales all year,” said Laura Reilly, the creator of the shopping newsletter Magasin, which spotlights sales twice a week year-round. “There’s just really nothing setting Black Friday apart, necessarily, as a sales season versus the rest of the year.”

item.title: Pressure Builds at American Airlines as It Lags Delta and United
item.description:
Late last month, thousands of American Airlines employees gathered online and at a ballroom at the company’s headquarters in Fort Worth, Texas, for an update on how the airline was doing. After executives recognized top performers, the proceedings turned sober.

Despite a nearly 20 percent jump in revenue from July through September, the company lost money in the quarter and things were not about to get better soon, the chief executive, Robert Isom, told his staff.

“We produced a loss for the quarter and we’re projecting a loss for the year,” he said. “All right, that’s just the plain old facts.”

American flies more passengers than any other U.S. carrier, yet over the last five years it has consistently lagged other big airlines in profits. This year, Wall Street analysts estimate the company will lose about $1 billion even as Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are expected to report profits of around $3 billion each, according to S&P Capital IQ.

A surge in jet fuel costs because of the war with Iran has hurt all airlines, but it has taken a particularly hard toll on American because it was already struggling. The company has a large debt accumulated in the years after its 2013 merger with US Airways and during the pandemic. It also made several strategic mistakes that have left it far behind Delta and United in courting affluent and business travelers.

Those struggles have drawn public rebukes from American’s pilots’ and flight attendants’ unions. Seizing on the company’s problems, United’s chief executive, Scott Kirby, who previously worked at American, floated a merger earlier this year to President Trump.

American and even Mr. Trump dismissed the idea, which has gone nowhere. But many in the industry say Mr. Isom and his team need to urgently make up the ground American has lost to Delta and United.

“We used to call the gap a canyon,” said Dennis Tajer, a spokesman for the pilots’ union at American, the Allied Pilots Association. “It’s an entirely different continent right now.”

American executives say they have a plan to turn things around, and analysts largely say it is making the right moves but is years behind. The airline is investing more in premium seats, Wi-Fi, airport lounges and better relationships with corporate customers. The big question now is whether American can change fast enough when Delta and United, which have deeper pockets, are also pursuing similar strategies.

One of American’s biggest problems is that travelers are willing to pay more to travel on Delta and United. According to estimates by Dan McKenzie, an airline analyst with Seaport Research Partners, Delta’s fares are 12 percent above the industry average on similar flights. United’s fares are 9 percent above average, while American’s are only 3 percent higher.

To match Delta and United’s profit margins, Mr. McKenzie estimates, American will need to bring in about $4.5 billion more in revenue every year.

American could make up some of that ground by getting more out of its loyalty program and branded credit cards, analysts said. Last year, Delta raked in more than $8 billion in payments from its credit card partnership with American Express. American collected more than $6 billion from its credit card and loyalty partners and now hopes to increase that by issuing credit cards only through Citi.

“We’ve underperformed for the past handful of years here,” Devon May, American’s chief financial officer, said in an interview, referring to revenue growth. “I expect that with our initiatives, we will be outperforming going forward.”

A big part of American’s turnaround plan involves undoing decisions made after its merger with US Airways. For example, the airline plans to add video screens to the backs of seats on more than 800 single-aisle jets, reversing a 2017 decision to save money by eliminating them. The screens won’t begin rolling out until 2028.

From 2014 to 2019, American also spent more than $12 billion buying back its own stock even as it was acquiring lots of new planes. By the time the pandemic upended air travel in 2020, the company had nearly $40 billion in debt and other long-term obligations. Like other airlines, American borrowed more to survive the pandemic.

During the pandemic, the airline retired dozens of larger planes used for international flights, counting on Boeing to deliver replacements on time. But Boeing fell behind, leaving American short of those planes when demand for international travel boomed two years later.

Analysts say American was also hurt by its smaller presence in rich coastal cities. For example, Delta and United each offer nearly twice as many seats flying out of New York as American, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

“You’ve got to own the right properties on the board to win the game,” Mr. McKenzie said. “Boardwalk is New York City.”

Setting aside debt and aircraft costs, company executives say American’s core business kept pace with United’s until 2023. That year, the airline made another big error by trying to compel business travelers to book tickets directly rather than through the corporate travel agencies they were accustomed to. After customers complained, the airline reversed course.

American has also fallen behind in reliability. In October, about 80 percent of American’s flights arrived on time, compared with nearly 87 percent for Delta and about 84 percent for United, according to Cirium.

“The most important thing that American Airlines can do to win back those customers is to operate a reliable airline,” said Henry Harteveldt, an airline industry analyst.

In November 2025, Nat Pieper, who spent much of his career at Delta and Northwest Airlines, joined American as chief commercial officer, overseeing its routes, sales and loyalty program. Days into the job, he met with senior leaders from about a dozen major travel agencies. After the 2023 change to corporate bookings, he recalled, there was unmistakable “tension in that room.”

But over the past year, American has worked to mend those relationships while investing in service, reliability and technology. By a follow-up meeting this fall, Mr. Pieper said the travel agents were much happier with the airline. A survey published this month by Business Travel News showed that corporate travel buyers are more satisfied with American, though the airline still ranked last among major carriers.

American says those efforts, combined with its investments in better amenities on planes and at airports, will help it win back customers who defected to other airlines. The airline also plans to roll out high-speed Starlink Wi-Fi starting next year. But making itself more appealing will require big investments. Even after cutting about $18 billion in debt, American still owes more than $36 billion.

Mr. Pieper and Mr. May said the real test for American will be in growing revenue per seat faster than its rivals — a feat they say they are confident about pulling off.

But in the third quarter, revenue per seat grew faster at Delta and United than at American, though only slightly. American had already missed the profit-margin goals it set in 2024, even before this year’s fuel price shock. Mr. May said American still aims to reach those targets. And analysts expect the airline to return to profitability next year.

Patience is wearing thin, particularly among employees. American set aside $55 million for profit-sharing payments in 2025. The comparable number at Delta was $1.3 billion and about $700 million at United. This year, leaders of the union that represents tens of thousands of flight attendants at American passed a symbolic no-confidence vote in Mr. Isom.

“They have the network to get there,” said Bill Swelbar, an aviation industry analyst. “They don’t have a balance sheet that gives them a lot of time.”

item.title: Luxury Water Is Luring Drinkers Who Have Lost Their Thirst for Alcohol
item.description:
When diners at Gwen, an upscale restaurant in Los Angeles, began seeking more nonalcoholic beverage options about three years ago, Martin Riese, a certified water sommelier, came up with a winelike menu for water.

The options include Vichy Catalan, a sparkling water from Spain, at $13 a bottle, and Castle Rock, a $12 bottle of still water sourced from spring water from California. (The restaurant serves filtered tap water from Los Angeles for free.)

Last year, the restaurant made nearly $100,000 in revenues from water sales. Drew Lucido, the general manager of Gwen, has never had so many people trying to sell him water, he said.

“We had a Japanese company that is trying to push into the U.S. market,” he said. “That blew my mind, coming all the way from Japan to sell me water.”

Bottled water is hot. No, not the water sold in mass retailers or grocery stores for $4 or $8 for a 12- or 24-pack of bottles. The market for premium-priced bottles and cans of still, sparkling and flavored sparkling water is booming. Analysts at Grand View Research expect the market for higher-priced waters to nearly double to $45.2 billion by 2033.

Alcohol consumption in the United States, by comparison, has declined over the past several years as people have turned to a variety of nonalcoholic beverages. Overall consumption of beer, wine, spirits and ready-to-drink mixes fell 5 percent last year, according to IWSR, a company that tracks the industry.

Mr. Riese, who tastes and judges waters around the world, is enthusiastic about hydration. He explained that water from a spring in Europe contains a mix of minerals, salts, metals and ions that is different from that of water from Arkansas. A water with a low minerality, for instance, can pair well with salads or sushi, Mr. Riese said.

“New Zealand sauvignon blanc tastes different than one created in California,” he said, comparing water to wine. “It’s the same grape, but it tastes different because it was raised in soils with different compositions.” Fine-water drinkers can discern the variation and are willing to pay for it, he said.

A host of newcomers are clamoring into the premium water arena, a space long occupied by brands like Fiji, Perrier, Evian and Voss. The new brands are leaning on clever marketing, unusual flavors or even razzle-dazzle science to capture the attention of Gen Z or younger consumers.

“If you talk to the big clubs in Miami, the kids are drinking more water than ever,” said Peter Carr, who spent much of his career in the beer and spirits industry at companies like Bacardi and Diageo.

Now, he’s the chief executive of Air Water Ventures, a start-up that uses special generators to draw humidity from the air to produce water. The cans and bottles of A1R water, priced from $3 to $7, are sold at various Miami hotels and clubs and at Miami Heat games and Inter Miami soccer matches.

“We’re trying to tap into the premium water consumer,” Mr. Carr said. “Someone who is into health and shops at Whole Foods, who cares about fitness.”

It’s not just affluent customers. Premium water brands are increasingly marketed to younger consumers, leaning into the concept that the products are part of a specific luxury experience or lifestyle.

“Grocery prices are going up, yet premium-priced items are still doing well,” said Scott Dicker, the head of research and insights at SPINS, a research firm. “The big picture is that people want more from their beverages.”

For years, the distinctive cobalt-blue glass bottles of Saratoga Spring Water typically graced white-linen-covered tables at upscale restaurants. But then the fitness influencer Ashton Hall began posting videos of himself doing push-ups next to a bottle of Saratoga, which can cost $2 to $4. As part of an early morning ritual, he filled a glass bowl with ice, lemons and Saratoga water and stuck his face in it. Repeatedly.

The videos spread on social media, introducing Saratoga to a new, younger audience. Sales soared for Saratoga’s owner, Primo Brands. The company tried but did not reach a partnership agreement with Mr. Hall. It formed marketing relationships with the BMX athlete Nigel Sylvester and the W.N.B.A. star Skylar Diggins instead.

“When we started to partner with people who reached younger consumers, they readily came into the brand,” Kheri Tillman, chief marketing officer at Primo Brands, said. “We found a way to make a high-end water really approachable for those moments and for those consumers.”

Revenue from its premium brands, Saratoga and Mountain Valley Spring Water, were up nearly 32 percent for the year through the end of September compared with a year ago. Shares of the company have surged nearly 50 percent this year.

Zach Knipe, 47, said he became “addicted” to Saratoga sparkling water years ago when he worked at an upscale steakhouse. While Mr. Knipe, now an account manager for an orthopedic surgical company who lives in Hershey, Pa., buys a variety of sparkling water in cans and bottles these days, Saratoga remains a favorite.

“The sparkling water stays colder in the glass bottles,” Mr. Knipe said. “I have a bottle of it in my fridge right now.”

The category of “water” is evolving well beyond still and sparkling. Brands are adding protein, fiber and even collagen to water to increase its functionality. Others are blurring the line between water and other beverages, including sodas.

It has been eight years since Liquid Death invigorated the water category through its tallboy aluminum cans featuring skull images, which were marketed through parody ads showing kids “shotgunning” the water. The bulk of the company’s sales comes from its fast-growing soda-flavored sparkling waters. There’s Mt. Death, designed to taste like Mountain Dew, and Doctor Death, which mimics Dr Pepper. Tallboy sizes contain no caffeine and have 20 calories and four grams of sugar.

Killer Cola, however, hasn’t been a big hit, admits Mike Cessario, the founder and chief executive of Liquid Death. “People go crazy about Coke or Pepsi,” he said. “That flavor was polarizing.”

Mr. Cessario isn’t worried about the new entrants in the premium space. “What differentiates us, as more brands come along, is that we’re one of the only plain water brands that’s getting young people, ages 5 to 16, excited to drink water,” he said.

New brands are focusing on the premium space because they need the higher prices to cover their costs, Mr. Cessario said. Mass-market water brands like Aquafina, which is owned by PepsiCo, or Dasani, which is owned by Coca-Cola, sell at lower prices, hoping to make money through volume.

But new companies have to “create a cool brand to justify the premium or a water with minute functional differences between your water and someone else’s,” Mr. Cessario said.

Sauna Water, a line of botanical sparkling “wellness” waters, is targeting consumers who go to saunas, explained Jeff Vondenkamp, who separated the water business from his brewery in Walker, Minn., about a year ago.

While he suggested that cans of his Nordic Spruce and Forest Fields water be priced around $4 a can, some retailers have charged more than $7 a can, he said. He’s also trying to expand into grocery store chains, where Sauna Water is likely to be priced closer to $3.50 a can, he said.

“We went in with a very specific target for this brand, very high-end,” Mr. Vondenkamp said. While he initially targeted saunas, Mr. Vondenkamp said the company has been doing a brisk business selling cans to bars, where the botanical-flavored waters are an alternative to alcohols like gin, but also to coffeehouses.

“I can go into almost any coffee shop in Minneapolis and they’ll say, ‘Sure, we’ll try it,’” Mr. Vondenkamp said. “The days of choice at a restaurant being a can of pop, apple juice and mineral water are behind us. Cafes are going to have 10, 12 or 14 different options of beverages.”

item.title: Putting Socially Conscious Investments in 401(k) Plans Could Get Harder
item.description:
The Labor Department proposed new rules on Monday that could potentially discourage 401(k)s and similar workplace savings programs from adding investment options that take into account environmental, social, and governance factors, often called E.S.G. investing.

It’s not the first time. The rules governing retirement savings accounts have continued to bounce around from one presidential administration to the next. For decades, successive Labor Departments — which oversee retirement plans — have provided guidance on how to consider these factors. The first Trump administration issued tighter rules around when E.S.G. concerns could be taken into consideration, which President Biden later modified.

The current Trump administration acknowledged the “regulatory ping-pong” before serving up a new regulation of its own, which emphasizes that plan administrators must focus on financial outcomes. The goal, the department said, was to restore neutrality.

“Our proposed rule makes clear that retirement plan fiduciaries must make investment decisions solely in the financial interests of workers and retirees, not to advance political or social agendas,” Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said in a statement.

The proposal clarifies the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, the 1974 law known as ERISA, which requires plan administrators to act solely in the best interests of employees. But presidential administrations have interpreted parts of it differently.

Experts said the latest proposal does not prohibit plan overseers from taking these factors into account if a prudent investment evaluation supports it. But the proposal stripped out language that reassured plan fiduciaries that considering the economic effects of climate change in an investment analysis (or other factors), for example, was permitted.

The proposal also eliminates a piece of the rule that said fiduciaries could use nonfinancial factors — such as E.S.G. considerations — to break a tie between two equivalent investments. Additionally, it erases a provision that said taking participant preferences into account, even if prudent, does not violate law.

“There would be less of a path for large 401(k) sponsors to incorporate E.S.G.- themed investments based, in part, on participant preferences,” said Jason Roberts, founding partner of the Fiduciary Law Center. “It could have a chilling effect.”

Lisa Gomez, the former assistant secretary of labor for the Employee Benefits Security Administration during the Biden administration, said that the proposal’s emphasis on maximizing benefits sounds protective of retirement savers’ interests. But she noted that ERISA already requires fiduciaries to act exclusively in participants’ interests.

“The question is whether this new approach provides meaningful additional protection or instead creates uncertainty and new opportunities to challenge fiduciary decisions based on alleged motives, even where the investment decision itself was financially prudent,” added Ms. Gomez, now president of LMG Collaborative Consulting Solutions.

“To me, the bigger risk is that fiduciaries become more defensive rather than more effective,” she continued. “That could mean less consideration of financially relevant information, fewer investment choices, and additional costs or litigation risks that ultimately affect workers.”

In a call with reporters, a Labor Department official said plan administration officials “may not have ulterior motives or collateral interests” when selecting investments. “And we believe that will inform all fiduciaries as to whether an impact fund or E.S.G. fund is appropriate for retirement funds,” the official said. “We believe the answer will be very rarely.”

The latest proposal follows another introduced in March, which paves the way for retirement plan administrators to add riskier alternative investments — from private equity to cryptocurrency — while lessening the regulatory burden and risks of lawsuits for sponsors. That proposal would allow plan sponsors to meet their fiduciary obligations as long as they followed a certain process, which requires them to evaluate investments using six factors, including performance, fees, complexity, among others.

Members of the public will have 60 days to comment on the latest proposal before it is finalized. After that, whether it has any staying power under future administrations remains an open question.

“What plan sponsors really need is a durable set of fiduciary principles they can follow regardless of which party occupies the White House,” said William Strange, a principal and consulting actuary at Milliman.

item.title: ‘Carthage Resident Al Gore’ Buys His Hometown Tennessee Newspaper
item.description:
Before he was a senator, and before he was vice president, Al Gore was a reporter. Now, he’s returning to journalism, as a newspaper owner. He is buying his hometown paper, The Carthage Courier, in Carthage, Tenn.

The announcement, which the paper published Monday under the headline “Carthage Courier Announces New Ownership,” was a departure from the grim procession of local newspapers that have closed or faced steep cutbacks in recent years. Since 2005, more than 3,500 newspapers have shuttered. On average, two close every week.

The Courier, a weekly newspaper, covers the towns of Carthage, South Carthage and Gordonsville in Smith County, a rural area that is home to about 20,000 people, about 55 miles east of Nashville.

The paper has been publishing since 1913, and has been owned by the Lake family since 1976. The family put the The Courier up for sale this fall, just before Geraldine Lake, its longtime owner, died this month at 84.

On Monday, the newspaper announced that the family was selling The Courier to “Carthage resident Al Gore.” An agreement formally transferring ownership of the paper to Mr. Gore, 78, who owns a farm in Carthage, is expected to be finalized in the coming weeks. A sale price was not disclosed.

Mr. Gore’s purchase of the paper, The Courier wrote, “ensures its 113-year legacy of community-focused news and information continues under local stewardship.”

Mr. Gore was not immediately available for an interview, an aide said on Tuesday. The son of a U.S. senator from Tennessee, he was a military reporter in Vietnam in 1971 and then spent five years covering breaking news, the police and investigative stories for The Tennessean newspaper in Nashville.

“Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at The Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community,” Mr. Gore said in a statement published by The Courier. “When my hometown paper came up for sale, I saw an opportunity to help preserve The Courier as an independent voice for Carthage and Smith County.”

Bill Woodard, the executive director of the Smith County Chamber of Commerce, said Mr. Gore had been involved in the restoration of another local business, the Hotel Walton, in Carthage. “Mr. Gore is doing quite a bit here locally,” he said, adding that “everything he has done so far has been very positive.”

Readers of The Courier, Mr. Woodard said, had been concerned that it could be sold to a corporate owner who would consolidate it with other local papers. So Mr. Gore, he said, “might actually be saving the paper,” and ensuring that it will “operate as usual.”

Mr. Gore’s entry into the ranks of newspaper owners was the latest chapter in the unusual career he has built after he lost the 2000 presidential election to George W. Bush.

In 2007, he won an Academy Award for “An Inconvenient Truth,” his documentary warning about the effects of climate change. Later that year, he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a United Nations network of scientists.

More recently, he has held the title of founder and chairman of the Climate Reality Project, a nonprofit that seeks solutions to climate change, and is a founding partner and chairman of Generation Investment Management, an investment management firm focused on sustainable development.

Dave Gould, the president of the Tennessee Press Association, said Mr. Gore’s purchase of The Courier was “the latest sign of investment in Tennessee’s local newspapers.” Local owners recently bought the newspaper in Chattanooga, and Tennessee-based companies have been buying newspapers and starting new ones in several counties, he said.

“Much of the national conversation about local news is about decline,” he said. But he added: “People who know their communities are choosing to own the local newspaper because they understand its value. Readers want to know what is happening in their schools, courthouses and city halls, and in the lives of their neighbors.”

The Carthage Courier said it would continue publication through the transition in ownership, and will retain all of its current employees.

Mr. Gore, in his statement, emphasized his commitment to the paper’s long-term health.

“I look forward to supporting the Carthage Courier team, many of whom have served this community for decades, as they continue to provide vital information and serve this community for generations to come,” he said.
